source_spans.locator: Memory & Cognition 11(3), published p.295, Abstract: substantial effects of both belief and logic are reported, with belief bias more marked on invalid than valid syllogisms
Memory & Cognition 11(3), published p.297, Experiment 1 materials: validity and conclusion believability are crossed, with half of valid and half of invalid conclusions believable

Memory & Cognition 11(3), published p.300, Experiment 2 results: significant main effects of believability and validity and a significant Belief x Validity interaction; belief-bias effect is more marked for invalid than valid syllogisms
Memory & Cognition 11(3), published p.301, Experiment 3 instructions: answer yes if and only if the conclusion logically follows from the stated information

Memory & Cognition 11(3), published p.302, General Discussion: large and consistent effects of belief bias and logical validity across experiments, with a consistent trend for interaction such that belief bias is more marked for invalid problems

conditions: categorical syllogisms cross formal validity with conclusion believability while controlling alternative response-bias explanations
population: student participants in the three experiments
task: judge yes or no whether a presented conclusion follows logically from the stated premises or passage information

nodes.description: whether the conclusion follows logically from the premises
whether the conclusion is believable or unbelievable independently of its formal validity
yes/no judgment accepting the conclusion as following from the stated information
task rule that a yes response is appropriate if and only if the conclusion logically follows from the stated information
factorial comparison crossing formal validity with conclusion believability and measuring acceptance responses

relations.description: acceptance judgments vary with both formal validity and conclusion believability
the believability effect on acceptance is larger for invalid than for valid syllogisms; this is significant in Experiments 1 and 2 and remains a same-direction trend in Experiment 3
the crossed validity-by-believability manipulation exposes the separate and interacting contributions of formal validity and conclusion believability to acceptance
the explicit task criterion constrains the normatively requested response to whether the conclusion follows logically from the stated information
